lessonPlan.title: The Lady, or the Tiger? unit
lessonPlan.author: Frank R. Stockton
lessonPlan.editionNote: Reading text: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_lady,_or_the_tiger?_and_other_stories/The_Lady,_or_the_Tiger? (revision 5766637), cleaned for Liber et Libri.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 6–10 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this story, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Lady, or the Tiger?.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Lady, or the Tiger?: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Short story: read whole in one 90-minute lesson (assign longer stories as pre-reading). Middle School prompts use the full text when the grade tags include 6–8; otherwise teacher-selected passages.
lessonPlan.schedule: One 90-minute lesson (the whole story), with an optional take-home essay
essentialQuestions: What does The Lady, or the Tiger? suggest about jealousy and love?
What does The Lady, or the Tiger? suggest about justice and chance?
What does The Lady, or the Tiger? suggest about choice?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the story.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.

Each prompt is tagged for Common Core, Indiana 2023, Dual Credit (Indiana College Core), AP and Cambridge where they apply.

wholeBookTest.title: The Lady, or the Tiger?: whole-book test

items.prompt: How does the king's arena decide guilt?
options: The accused opens one of two doors

items.prompt: What is behind the two doors?
Why is the princess's lover on trial?
Which door does the princess point to?

options: It asks the reader which came out

items.prompt: In the line “He was a man of exuberant fancy, and, withal, of an authority so irresistible that, at his will, he turned his varied fancies into facts.”, what does “exuberant” most nearly mean?
options: indirect in departing from the accepted or proper way; misleading
a sloping gallery with seats for spectators (as in an operating room or theater)

items.prompt: In the line “It involves a study of the human heart which leads us through devious mazes of passion, out of which it is difficult to find our way.”, what does “devious” most nearly mean?
options: indirect in departing from the accepted or proper way; misleading
a sloping gallery with seats for spectators (as in an operating room or theater)

items.prompt: As used in the story (“He was a man of exuberant fancy, and, withal, of an authority so irresistible that, at his will, he turned his varied fancies into facts.”), what does “exuberant” mean?
options: decided by fate; leading to an unhappy end
be contingent upon (something that is elided)

items.prompt: As used in the story (“It involves a study of the human heart which leads us through devious mazes of passion, out of which it is difficult to find our way.”), what does “devious” mean?
options: indirect in departing from the accepted or proper way; misleading
pause or hold back in uncertainty or unwillingness
a sloping gallery with seats for spectators (as in an operating room or theater)

items.prompt: As used in the story (“How in her grievous reveries had she gnashed her teeth, and torn her hair, when she saw his start of rapturous delight as he opened the door”), what does “gnashed” mean?
options: assumptions an argument is based on
decided by fate; leading to an unhappy end

items.prompt: As used in the story (“This vast amphitheatre, with its encircling galleries, its mysterious vaults, and its unseen passages, was an agent of poetic justice, in wh”), what does “amphitheatre” mean?
options: be contingent upon (something that is elided)
indirect in departing from the accepted or proper way; misleading
a sloping gallery with seats for spectators (as in an operating room or theater)

items.prompt: As used in the story (“The king and his court were in their places, opposite the twin doors,—those fateful portals, so terrible in their similarity.”), what does “fateful” mean?
options: decided by fate; leading to an unhappy end
pause or hold back in uncertainty or unwillingness
assumptions an argument is based on

shortAnswer: Explain how jealousy and love develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how justice and chance develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
Explain how choice develops from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two passages.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the story's central concerns (jealousy and love, justice and chance, choice) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what The Lady, or the Tiger? teaches about jealousy and love. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Frank R. Stockton develops jealousy and love in The Lady, or the Tiger?. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Frank R. Stockton develops jealousy and love across The Lady, or the Tiger?. Trace the idea through at least three parts of the story and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of The Lady, or the Tiger? (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of jealousy and love. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of jealousy and love in The Lady, or the Tiger?. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Frank R. Stockton's choices in The Lady, or the Tiger? (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of jealousy and love, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places The Lady, or the Tiger?'s treatment of jealousy and love in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on jealousy and love in The Lady, or the Tiger? that reads the story against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on jealousy and love in The Lady, or the Tiger?. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about jealousy and love in The Lady, or the Tiger?, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on jealousy and love in The Lady, or the Tiger?, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
